newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Moldovan minister to discuss old arms with Russia.
newsitem.headline: Moldovan minister to discuss old arms with Russia.

text.p: The defence minister of ex-Soviet Moldova said on Friday he was confident that talks with Russia would produce agreement on disposing of World War Two vintage ammunition stocked in its separatist Dnestr region.

Valeriu Pasat goes to Moscow next week for talks also likely to study plans to destroy the 200 tonnes of munitions. Dnestr leaders, who fought the Chisinau government in 1992 and signed a peace pact only this year, oppose the scheme.

"These are particularly dangerous because much larger quantities of more modern ammunition are located nearby," Pasat told a news conference in Bucharest after talks with Romanian defence minister Victor Babiuc.
"We believe we will find a way to discuss this with Dnestr officials. They have not agreed to have the ammunitions blown up on their own territory. This is not just our concern, but Russia's too."
Moldova, most of which belonged to Romania before World War Two, signed an accord with the breakaway Slav-dominated Dnestr region in May, with Russia and Ukraine helping in mediation.
But little progress has since been made in establishing the region's status. Moldova maintains Dnestr is part of its territory and Dnestr leaders speak of two separate entities.
Dnestr's leaders proclaimed independence from Moldova in 1990, a year before the Soviet Union collapsed, as a pre-emptive move against fears that Moldova might merge with Romania.
Fighting between Dnestr forces and Moldova's newly independent army killed several hundred people in 1992 before it was halted with the help of the Russian army.
The army is to leave under a pact signed in 1994 by Moldova and Russia but still not ratified by the Russian parliament.
Pasat, the only civilian defence minister in former Soviet territory outside the three Baltic states, toured the Dnestr region last month despite objections from local leaders.

The weaponry at issue is on territory controlled by the Russian 14th Army but Dnestr leaders have tried to lay claim to it or secure compensatory concessions, including a reduction in debts incurred for imported Russian natural gas.

About 60 percent of Moldova's 4.5 million people are ethnic Romanians. But enthusiasm for unification, which swelled after the fall of communism, is now confined to a small minority of nationalists on both sides of the border.
